Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} reports, for each family--mechanism cell and
regime, the empirical coverage of the central 95\% interval and the mean
error for period life expectancy at birth and at 65 and for the annuity-due
factor at 65 and 2\%, each computed on the period table of the first test
year from the cell's own sample paths and compared with the same functional
of the observed rates. The functionals are taken from the latent rate paths
of every distributional cell, before the Poisson composition that the
rate-scale scores use. Conformal cells have no such paths---their samples
are uniform draws inside a band, a convention for interval metrics only---so
their derived-quantity rows are not applicable and the table marks them
\emph{n/a} rather than tabulating a distributional claim. \Hfive\ is
restricted by Addendum~3 (\S8) to the ex-post coverage of these derived
intervals, with the attenuation alternative---that life-table integration
averages a rate-surface failure away---as the named competitor. Both
outcomes are informative: the first says the reserve is wrong, the second
says the audit's headline is a statement about rates rather than about
liabilities. \todo{result pending} \todo{attach the citation for the

\subsection{Reading a coverage shortfall in balance-sheet terms}

For an annuity-due of one per annum at age 65, the interval on $\annuity$
translates directly into an interval on the best-estimate liability of a
unit annuitant. A nominal 95\% interval that covers the realised
$\annuity$ in materially fewer than 95\% of population--sex cells is, in
Solvency~II language, an internal model whose longevity distribution is
too narrow; the shortfall of the model's 97.5\% quantile of $\annuity$
below the realised value, where it occurs, is the amount by which the
implied capital at that level is understated. We report this quantity as a
proportion of the central $\annuity$ so that it is portable across
populations and interest-rate assumptions. \todo{compute from the
$\annuity$ point, upper-quantile and realised columns of the results files
once Table~\ref{tab:h5-actuarial} exists; decide whether a worked example
on a hypothetical portfolio adds anything}

\subsection{The longevity tail}

The 99.5\% upper quantile of the predictive distribution of $\annuity$ is
the one-year longevity tail an internal model would carry. The fraction of
cells in which the realised value exceeds the model's own 99.5\% quantile
is the empirical frequency of a nominally once-in-200-year event, and is the
quantity the pandemic years let us observe for the first time. This is
descriptive and not a registered hypothesis. \todo{the runner emits only
the 2.5\% and 97.5\% sample quantiles of the derived quantities; a 99.5\%
column must be added to the runner and the cells re-scored before this
paragraph can be filled}
